newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil pleased with Eurolire reception.
newsitem.headline: Brazil pleased with Eurolire reception.

text.p: Brazil's Central Bank Tuesday welcomed the pricing of its 500 billion lire 20-year Eurobond, saying it was indicative of a divergence in risk appraisal between investors and the rating agencies, an official said.

Fernando Antonio Gomes, head of the Central Bank's foreign capital department, told reporters the issue was sold at par with an 11 percent coupon, giving it a spread over equivalent U.S. Treasuries of 348 basis points.
The official said Brazil's Eurolire priced at exactly the same spread as an identical lire bond issued by Mexico on April 17.
Standard & Poor's Corp recently raised Brazil's sovereign credit rating to BB-minus from B-plus. But it still rates Mexico a notch higher at BB.

"We had expected our spread to come in a bit above Mexico but in the end got the same. We got the same conditions as Mexico did recently which shows clearly that investors see Brazil in a better light than the rating agencies," Gomes said.
The 20-year Italian lire issue, its first with that maturity, almost completes Brazil's quest to plant sovereign benchmarks all along its yield curve.
Offers for a 30-year global, tied to a Brady buyback and swap deal, were pouring in Tuesday and the result of that placement was expected to be announced Wednesday in New York.

"The lengthening of the maturity serves as a benchmark on Brazil's yield curve and reflects the greater confidence of investors, prepared to pay for papers of longer maturities albeit with higher returns," the Central Bank said in a statement.
Gomes said Brazil had passed "its first long term test" with the warm reception for the Italian lire Eurobond.
He said 70 percent of the paper had been sold in the retail market and 30 percent placed with institutional investors.

The markets had originally expected the launch to take place in May. But Gomes said Brazil decided to hold out till June because there were no other sovereign issuers planning placements in that market this month.
The revenue, which amounts to about $300 million, will be used exclusively to retire more expensive domestic debt.
Gomes said Brazil was likely to take a break from Eurobond operations until September because of the Northern Hemisphere's summer holidays.
When it came back to the market, maturities of over three years were the most likely option.
"I think from now on the issues will be three to five years and over," Gomes said.
Over the past two years, Brazil has launched two, three, five and 10-year bonds in dollars, yen, marks, sterling, escudos and now lire.
It has also issued fungible Eurobonds in Austrian schilling, French francs and Dutch guilders. Fungible means the bonds can redenominate into the euro after European Monetary Union.
